defects.detail: "bit-manipulation/basic-bit-ops" holds 0 problems while "bit-manipulation/xor-properties" — which builds on it — holds 4. (Dependency is a curriculum judgement, not repository metadata.)

8 problems, none Easy (M2 H6) — a learner meets this pattern for the first time at Medium.

Two patterns for the same technique in different topics. The stack-queue one is empty; the sliding-window one holds the repo's largest concentration of Hard problems. [measured: stack-queue/monotonic-deque=0, sliding-window-two-pointers/monotonic-deque-window=8]

Three-way partition. The arrays pattern is empty, but sort-colors — the canonical Dutch-flag problem — is already authored under opposite-direction-two-pointers. [measured: arrays/dutch-national-flag=0, sliding-window-two-pointers/opposite-direction-two-pointers=12]

Four linked-list problems are authored under a two-pointer pattern because the linked-list topic is harness-blocked. NOT relocated in 3A.1 — see REQUIRES_REAUTHOR_AFTER_NODE_ENCODING: relocation alone is insufficient because a cycle cannot be represented in a flat array at all. [measured: sliding-window-two-pointers/same-direction-two-pointers=12]

seed-learning.js is upsert-only (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (slug) DO UPDATE) and has no delete pass. Removing a problem from a seed file therefore leaves the row in the database, and problems-index keeps serving it. The divergence is silent: no gate compares the database against the seed files. CONSEQUENCE: Any content deletion has to be done twice, and forgetting the second half ships a problem that exists for users but has no source of truth. FIX: Either a reconciling delete pass in the seeder, or a drift check that fails when the database holds a problem slug no seed file declares. Not built in 3A.2A: it is infrastructure and that phase is content.

The literal-based harness embeds each argument as source, capped at MAX_LITERAL_BYTES = 24,000 bytes, which is roughly 4,000 integers. Any problem that reaches `long long` only because the INPUT is large is therefore unauthorable: inversion counting needs n > 65,536 to exceed int32, and that array renders to about 400KB of Java or C source. CONSEQUENCE: `long long`, `vector<long long>`, `vector<double>` and `vector<bool>` are still implemented, unit-tested, and never executed on a provider. The 3A.1 blueprint expected inversion counting to close that gap and it cannot. FIX: Reach the wide types with a SMALL input and a large answer instead — a product over a handful of values, or a bit-shift result — rather than a large input and a counted answer. Recommended for 3A.2B; not invented during 3A.2A because it is not a blueprint slot.

Three v2 problem files have no authoring spec: arrays/kadane-maximum-subarray, stack-queue/parenthesis-matching, sliding-window-two-pointers/variable-size-sliding-window. build-authored-problems.js rewrites `<pattern>.json` wholesale from the spec, so creating a spec for one of those patterns would ERASE the existing problem unless it is re-authored into the spec at the same time. CONSEQUENCE: A trap for exactly the patterns the 150 milestone tops up. Hit deliberately rather than accidentally: the kadane spec re-authors maximum-subarray so it is not lost. FIX: Bring all v2 files under the pipeline, which is the same work as defect D7.

the statement says the answer may be returned "in any order" and then requires a specific one. The grader compares with an exact deepEqual, so only the specific order is accepted and the first clause is false. Wording fix, no behaviour change.

analysis.disclaimer: Judgement, not repository data. No company-frequency figures are used anywhere.

basics/complexity-analysis.why: Every later pattern is chosen by cost. Also the one pattern that may not be expressible as a graded function — see the notes.
basics/complexity-analysis.kind_reason: Deriving an asymptotic bound is assessed by explanation. A function that returns a complexity string tests string formatting, not analysis.

basics/simulation.why: Translating prose into a correct loop is the skill every other topic assumes.

basics/integer-math-modular.why: Needed by hashing, overflow safety and modular DP; nothing in the current curriculum is blocked on it.

basics/prefix-arithmetic-basics.why: Direct prerequisite of arrays/prefix-sum, which is the most populated non-window pattern.

basics/sieve-and-primes.why: Number theory. Self-contained and nothing depends on it.

basics/bit-and-base-conversion.why: Prerequisite for bit-manipulation, which currently starts at xor-properties with no groundwork.

sorting/comparison-sorts-elementary.why: You cannot reason about "just sort it" until you have written one.

sorting/merge-sort-divide-conquer.why: The divide-and-conquer shape is reused by k-way merge, inversion counting and quickselect reasoning.

sorting/quick-sort-and-partition.why: Partitioning is the mechanism behind quickselect, which is the optimal answer to top-k.

sorting/heap-sort.why: Bridges sorting to heaps; useful but replaceable by the heap topic itself.

sorting/non-comparison-sorts.why: Counting and bucket sort underpin several frequency problems.

sorting/custom-comparator-and-stability.why: Greedy and interval problems are almost all "sort by the right key first"; stability is where they silently break.

arrays/prefix-sum.why: Range-query thinking, and the hashmap-of-prefixes trick generalises widely.

arrays/difference-array.why: Range-update dual of prefix sum. Real but narrower.

arrays/kadane-maximum-subarray.why: The canonical entry point to optimal-substructure thinking; a gateway to DP.

arrays/in-place-rearrangement.why: O(1)-space discipline, asked constantly and easy to get subtly wrong.

arrays/cyclic-sort.why: Value-as-index trick for the missing/duplicate family. Elegant but narrow.

arrays/dutch-national-flag.why: Three-way partition. Note the curriculum already teaches it elsewhere — see the duplicate finding.

arrays/intervals.why: Merge/insert intervals is a first-tier interview pattern and the topic is empty.

binary-search/lower-upper-bound.why: Boundary discipline. Every other binary-search pattern is this with a predicate swapped, and getting it wrong is the usual cause of off-by-one bugs.

binary-search/binary-search-on-2d-matrix.why: Index flattening. A representation trick more than a new technique.

binary-search/binary-search-on-answer.why: Searching a monotone predicate rather than an array is the highest-leverage idea in the topic and it is empty.

binary-search/peak-and-bitonic.why: Binary search without a sorted array; good for breaking the "must be sorted" assumption.

strings/frequency-counter.why: Counting is the base string technique. Populated.

strings/palindrome-expansion.why: Centre expansion is the standard non-DP palindrome tool and the pattern is empty.

strings/kmp-failure-function.why: Needs prefix-function reasoning that nothing else in the curriculum builds toward yet.

strings/z-algorithm.why: Competitive-programming technique; rarely expected in interviews.

strings/rolling-hash-rabin-karp.why: Depends on integer-math-modular, which is itself empty.

strings/manacher-palindromes.why: Highly specialised; palindrome-expansion and DP cover interview needs.

linked-list/dummy-node.why: The standard way to avoid head special-casing.

linked-list/cycle-detection-floyd.why: Canonical, and the repo already has a cautionary version of it modelled as an array.

recursion/subset-include-exclude.why: The include/exclude decision tree is the shape every backtracking and knapsack problem reuses.

recursion/permutation-swap.why: Ordering enumeration, and the in-place swap variant teaches state restoration.

recursion/backtracking-with-restore.why: Explicit undo is where most candidates break; a distinct skill from plain recursion.

recursion/divide-and-conquer.why: Overlaps sorting/merge-sort but generalises the recurrence.

recursion/decision-tree.why: Framing device for turning a problem into branching choices.

recursion/recursion-on-data-structures.why: The bridge to trees — but it needs a linked or tree structure, so it is harness-blocked.

bit-manipulation/basic-bit-ops.why: Mask/shift/test primitives. Empty while xor-properties has four problems, which is backwards.

bit-manipulation/count-set-bits.why: Popcount and Brian Kernighan; also a DP-over-bits warm-up.

bit-manipulation/subset-enumeration-bitm.why: Needs both subsets and bit fluency.

bit-manipulation/bitmask-dp-state.why: Requires DP plus bitmask; two prerequisites deep.

stack-queue/parenthesis-matching.why: The introductory reason a stack exists. Only one problem.

stack-queue/monotonic-deque.why: Duplicated by sliding-window/monotonic-deque-window, which holds twelve problems — see the duplicate finding.

stack-queue/expression-evaluation.why: Parsing with two stacks; a genuinely different use of the structure.

stack-queue/stack-with-aggregate.why: Min-stack. Conceptually core, but it is a DESIGN problem and the harness models single functions — see the notes.

stack-queue/queue-from-stacks.why: Amortised analysis made concrete. Also design-shaped.

sliding-window-two-pointers/variable-siz.why: The grow/shrink invariant is the single most transferable window idea, and it has ONE problem while its neighbours have twelve.

sliding-window-two-pointers/opposite-dir.why: Converging pointers on sorted data. Twelve problems.

sliding-window-two-pointers/same-directi.why: Read/write pointer and in-place filtering. Twelve problems.

sliding-window-two-pointers/monotonic-de.why: Twelve problems, seven of them Hard — the most advanced material in the repo sitting in a topic whose prerequisites are unbuilt.

heaps/top-k-with-heap.why: Bounded-heap selection, one of the most reused shapes there is.

heaps/k-way-merge.why: Merging sorted streams under a heap.

heaps/scheduling-with-heap.why: Interval plus heap; needs arrays/intervals first.

heaps/heap-as-priority-queue.why: What a heap is and what it costs. Prerequisite for the rest of the topic and for dijkstra.

heaps/heap-dijkstra-shape.why: Belongs after graphs traversal is established.

greedy/sort-then-greedy.why: The base greedy move. Empty while interval-scheduling, which is a specialisation of it, has four problems.

greedy/exchange-argument.why: A proof technique rather than a coding pattern; hard to assess by unit tests.
greedy/exchange-argument.kind_reason: Proving a greedy choice is safe is a proof obligation. Any function wrapping it would grade the implementation of an algorithm the learner was told to use, which is the opposite of the skill.

greedy/gas-station-circular.why: Prefix-minimum reasoning on a circular array.

greedy/jump-game-greedy.why: Reachability frontier; the standard greedy-versus-DP comparison.

binary-trees/dfs-traversals.why: Pre/in/post order is the alphabet of every tree problem.

binary-trees/bfs-level-order.why: Level structure; bridges to graph BFS.

binary-trees/tree-recursion-with-return.why: Returning aggregates up the recursion is the core tree skill.

bst/in-order-property.why: Everything about a BST follows from in-order being sorted.

graphs/bfs-shortest-path.why: Unweighted shortest path. Empty while dfs-connectivity has four, which inverts the usual teaching order.

graphs/topological-sort.why: Dependency ordering plus cycle detection on a DAG.

graphs/union-find.why: Disjoint sets; the alternative lens on connectivity and a prerequisite for MST.

graphs/dijkstra.why: Needs heaps and BFS both established first.

graphs/mst-prim-kruskal.why: Needs union-find or heaps; narrow interview surface.

dynamic-programming/2d-grid.why: The natural step from 1-D, and the easiest place to see a table.

dynamic-programming/0-1-knapsack.why: Subset-sum family; the most reused DP formulation.

dynamic-programming/unbounded-knapsack.why: Coin-change variant; a loop-order change from 0-1.

dynamic-programming/lis-and-lcs.why: Subsequence DP, and LIS has the binary-search optimisation worth teaching.

dynamic-programming/edit-distance-and-al.why: Two-string DP; a clean generalisation of LCS.

dynamic-programming/interval-and-partiti.why: Interval recurrences need solid 2-D DP first.

tries/character-trie-basics.why: Prefix structure; inherently a design/class problem, so harness-shaped rather than importance-limited.

tries/prefix-and-autocomplete.why: The main practical use of a trie.

conceptual_patterns.basics/complexity-analysis: Deriving an asymptotic bound is assessed by explanation. A function that returns a complexity string tests string formatting, not analysis.
conceptual_patterns.greedy/exchange-argument: Proving a greedy choice is safe is a proof obligation. Any function wrapping it would grade the implementation of an algorithm the learner was told to use, which is the opposite of the skill.

analysis.pattern_dependencies_source: JUDGEMENT — patterns/*.json carries no prerequisites field

NODE_ENCODING.label: harness has no node type
NODE_ENCODING.detail: Arguments are decoded into the canonical type vocabulary, which has no encoding for a node with pointers. Passing a list or tree as a flat array yields problems solvable without the algorithm they teach — the repo already contains that mistake as linked-list-cycle, sitting in same-direction-two-pointers.

DESIGN_SHAPED.label: needs a class/multi-method signature
DESIGN_SHAPED.detail: The signature model is one function with typed arguments and one return. A problem whose whole point is a stateful object with several methods (min-stack, a queue built from stacks, a trie, a median stream) cannot be expressed, and flattening it into one call removes the thing being taught.

NOT_A_GRADED_FUNCTION.label: not naturally a graded function
NOT_A_GRADED_FUNCTION.detail: Reasoning about asymptotic cost, or proving an exchange argument, is assessed by explanation rather than by a return value. Forcing it into a unit-tested function produces a problem that tests something other than the skill.

linked-list-cycle.why: A cycle is not representable in a flat array. The problem as it stands can be solved without cycle detection, so relocating it would move a broken problem into the right folder. It must be re-authored against a genuine node representation.

linked-list-cycle-ii.why: Same defect as linked-list-cycle, and it additionally has to return the entry node of the cycle — which has no meaning without a node type.

middle-of-the-linked-list.why: As an array this is index arithmetic and teaches nothing about pointers; the fast/slow technique is only necessary when you cannot index. Faithful only with a node type.

remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.why: Array removal is a splice. The lesson is pointer rewiring with a gap of n, which needs a node type.

slots.concept: Increment a big-integer represented as a digit array, propagating carry
slots.objective: Translate a prose rule into a reverse-order loop with a carry invariant
slots.notRedundant: No existing problem manipulates a digit-array representation; prefix-sum problems read the array, they do not restructure it.

slots.concept: Reverse the digits of a signed 32-bit integer, refusing values that would overflow
slots.objective: Detect overflow BEFORE it happens rather than after
slots.notRedundant: Overflow-safe arithmetic appears nowhere in the current 96.
slots.int64: bounded — the answer is int32 by construction, but the check needs 64-bit reasoning; constrain input to int32

constraint.canonical: input and output both confined to signed 32-bit, returning 0 when the reversal would not fit
constraint.legitimate: Yes, and nothing is constrained. Worth recording only because the lesson is asymmetric across languages: in C/C++/Java/C# the check is genuinely necessary, while in JavaScript and Python the intermediate never overflows, so those two solve it by comparing against the 32-bit bound rather than by avoiding an overflow.

slots.concept: Convert an integer to its Roman-numeral form
slots.objective: Simulate repeated greedy subtraction against an ordered value table
slots.notRedundant: No existing problem builds an output string by consuming an input quantity; it is also the first place a lookup table drives the loop.

slots.concept: Greatest common divisor by the Euclidean algorithm
slots.objective: Reduce a problem by a recurrence on remainders
slots.notRedundant: Nothing in the curriculum does number theory.

slots.concept: Raise a value to an integer power by squaring, handling a negative exponent
slots.objective: Halve the exponent each step instead of multiplying n times
slots.notRedundant: The only divide-and-halve recurrence outside binary search, and one of very few problems using the `double` type — currently exercised by exactly one seeded problem.

slots.concept: Count trailing zeroes in a factorial without computing it
slots.objective: Reason about prime factors instead of evaluating
slots.notRedundant: Teaches avoiding the big value entirely — directly relevant to the 64-bit ceiling.

slots.concept: Running maximum of a sequence
slots.objective: See a prefix as any associative fold, not only a sum
slots.notRedundant: arrays/prefix-sum is entirely sum-based; this generalises the operator.

slots.concept: Answer one range-sum query from a precomputed prefix table
slots.objective: Separate the precompute step from the query step
slots.notRedundant: The existing running-sum problem RETURNS the prefix array; this one uses it to answer a query, which is the actual point of the technique.
slots.signature: vector<int> nums, int left, int right -> int

slots.concept: Count the split positions where the left part's sum is at least the right part's
slots.objective: Use a running prefix against a fixed total, so each split is answered in constant time
slots.notRedundant: find-pivot-index asks for one index where the two sides are EQUAL and returns it; this counts every position satisfying an INEQUALITY, which is the running-prefix-versus-total form rather than a search.

slots.concept: Sort an array with an explicit insertion sort
slots.objective: Write a sort rather than call one, and see the O(N^2) cost
slots.notRedundant: Every existing problem calls a library sort or avoids sorting.

slots.concept: Count the swaps a bubble sort performs, with early termination
slots.objective: Connect an operation count to the asymptotic bound
slots.notRedundant: Makes cost measurable, which is the assessable half of complexity-analysis.

slots.concept: Sort an array with merge sort
slots.objective: Split, recurse, merge — and see why the merge is the whole algorithm
slots.notRedundant: First divide-and-conquer recurrence in the curriculum.

slots.concept: Count inversions in an array using the merge step
slots.objective: Extract a quantity from a sort rather than the sorted order
slots.notRedundant: The first problem where the sort is a means rather than the goal — the merge step counts pairs it would otherwise just move.

slots.concept: Sort values by descending frequency, breaking ties by value
slots.objective: Sort by a derived key and make the tie-break explicit
slots.notRedundant: strings/sort-characters-by-frequency does this for characters only; this is the general integer form and states the tie-break, which that one leaves implicit.
slots.ordering: Fully determined: descending frequency, then ascending value. The tie-break is the lesson, so it is stated rather than left free.

slots.concept: Arrange integers to form the largest possible concatenated number
slots.objective: Recognise a comparator that is not a numeric comparison
slots.notRedundant: The comparator is on string concatenation, which is where "just sort descending" fails; nothing else teaches that.
slots.int64: returns a STRING deliberately — the numeric value would exceed the ceiling, and the string form sidesteps it legitimately rather than by constraint

constraint.canonical: the concatenation of up to 100 numbers, which as an integer would be hundreds of digits
constraint.robinhood: unchanged — the answer is returned as a STRING, so no numeric range applies
constraint.legitimate: Yes, and by representation rather than by constraint. The canonical problem returns a string too, precisely because the value does not fit any integer type. This is the shape to prefer whenever it is available: change what is returned, not what is asked.

slots.concept: Enumerate all subsets of a distinct-element array
slots.objective: See the binary include/exclude decision tree
slots.notRedundant: No enumeration problem exists in the curriculum at all.
slots.ordering: REQUIRED — subsets have no natural order. Each subset ascending, the outer list sorted by length then lexicographically. Follows the 3sum precedent.

slots.concept: Enumerate subsets of an array containing duplicates, without repeats
slots.objective: Prune a branch by sorting first and skipping equal siblings
slots.notRedundant: Deduplication during recursion is a distinct skill from the plain enumeration.
slots.ordering: REQUIRED — same convention as the distinct case, so the two problems are directly comparable.

slots.concept: Count subsets summing to a target, without enumerating them
slots.objective: Separate counting from enumeration — the step that makes DP possible
slots.notRedundant: Chosen so the pattern is not entirely C-unsupported, and it is the direct bridge to 0-1 knapsack.

slots.concept: All combinations of candidates summing to a target, reuse allowed
slots.objective: Mutate shared state and undo it on the way out
slots.notRedundant: First problem requiring an explicit undo step.
slots.ordering: REQUIRED — each combination non-decreasing, outer list sorted lexicographically.

slots.concept: All letter strings a digit sequence could spell on a phone keypad
slots.objective: Backtrack over a mapping rather than over the input array
slots.notRedundant: Returns strings, so it keeps the pattern reachable in C and varies the branching source.
slots.ordering: REQUIRED — lexicographic, which is also what a straightforward recursion produces if the keypad is walked in order.

slots.concept: Merge a list of overlapping intervals
slots.objective: Sort by start, then extend or emit
slots.notRedundant: greedy/interval-scheduling COUNTS or selects intervals; none of its four problems produces a merged set.
slots.ordering: Determined by the algorithm: ascending by start. Stated anyway so it is not accidental.

slots.concept: Insert one interval into a sorted disjoint set
slots.objective: Handle before/overlap/after as three explicit phases
slots.notRedundant: A single insertion has a different structure from a full merge.

slots.concept: Minimum number of rooms needed for overlapping meetings
slots.objective: Convert intervals into a sweep over start/end events
slots.notRedundant: The existing meeting-rooms asks whether ANY overlap exists (a boolean); this asks for maximum concurrency, which needs a sweep.

slots.concept: Maximum product of a contiguous subarray
slots.objective: Carry two running extremes because a negative flips them
slots.notRedundant: The existing maximum-subarray is additive and never needs the min tracked.
slots.int64: CONSTRAIN — cap n and |value| so the product stays inside the exact-integer range

constraint.canonical: LeetCode guarantees the answer fits a 32-bit integer — this is the CANONICAL constraint, not a Robinhood invention
constraint.robinhood: the same: bound n and |value| so the product stays within int32
constraint.legitimate: Yes. The lesson is carrying two running extremes because a negative value swaps them; overflow is not part of it, and the canonical problem already excludes overflow by construction.

slots.concept: Maximum subarray sum in a circular array
slots.objective: Decompose into the non-wrapping case and its complement
slots.notRedundant: Introduces the total-minus-minimum complement trick.

slots.concept: Leftmost insertion position for a target among duplicates
slots.objective: Make the loop return a boundary, not a hit
slots.notRedundant: The existing search-insert-position assumes distinct values, so it never exercises the duplicate boundary that makes lower-bound different from a plain search.

slots.concept: First and last index of a target in a sorted array
slots.objective: Compose lower and upper bound into a range
slots.notRedundant: Requires both boundaries, which no existing problem does.

slots.concept: For each query, count sorted values strictly below it
slots.objective: Reuse one sorted structure across many queries
slots.notRedundant: Introduces amortising a precomputation over a query set.
slots.ordering: Determined: one answer per query, in query order.

slots.concept: Smallest ship capacity that clears all packages within a day budget
slots.objective: Binary search a monotone predicate rather than an array
slots.notRedundant: The single biggest conceptual jump in the topic and no existing problem searches anything but an index.

slots.concept: Minimum hourly rate to finish all piles within an hour budget
slots.objective: Recognise the same predicate shape in different prose
slots.notRedundant: Deliberately the same technique with different framing — recognising that is the learning objective.

slots.concept: Shortest subarray whose sum reaches a target
slots.objective: Grow to satisfy, shrink to minimise
slots.notRedundant: The pattern holds exactly one problem (longest substring without repeats) and that one MAXIMISES; this minimises, which is the other half of the invariant.

slots.concept: Longest substring obtainable by replacing at most k characters
slots.objective: Keep a window valid against a derived quantity, not a raw count
slots.notRedundant: Window validity depends on window length minus max frequency — distinct from the at-most-k-distinct problems in at-most-k-window.

slots.concept: Smallest window of a string containing all characters of a pattern
slots.objective: Combine a frequency map with a shrinking window
slots.notRedundant: The canonical hard case of the pattern, and the pattern currently has no Hard problem at all.
slots.ordering: The window is unique in length but not necessarily in position; the statement must require the LEFTMOST shortest window.

slots.concept: Count palindromic substrings by expanding around each centre
slots.objective: Handle odd and even centres as one loop
slots.notRedundant: The existing valid-palindrome problems VERIFY a palindrome; none constructs or counts them.

slots.concept: Longest palindromic substring
slots.objective: Track the best centre rather than a running count
slots.notRedundant: Returns the substring, so it exercises string construction rather than counting.
slots.ordering: Ties are possible, so the statement must require the leftmost longest substring.

slots.concept: Number of set bits for every integer from 0 to n
slots.objective: Test and shift individual bits, and notice the recurrence
slots.notRedundant: xor-properties has four problems but the topic never teaches masking or shifting; this is the missing groundwork.

slots.concept: Reverse the bits of a 32-bit unsigned value
slots.objective: Build a result bit by bit while consuming the input
slots.notRedundant: Forces explicit bit placement rather than counting.
slots.int64: return must be long long — an unsigned 32-bit result exceeds int32 range while staying JSON-safe

constraint.canonical: input and output are unsigned 32-bit, so the result reaches 4294967295
constraint.robinhood: unchanged, but the RETURN type is `long long` because the canonical vocabulary has no unsigned type and 4294967295 exceeds int32
constraint.legitimate: Yes. The value is well inside the exact-integer range; only the declared type changes, and it changes to remain truthful about the range rather than to dodge a limit.

slots.concept: Minimum insertions to make a bracket string balanced
slots.objective: Track a deficit counter instead of a full stack
slots.notRedundant: The pattern has one problem, a boolean check; this asks for a quantity and shows the stack can collapse to a counter.

slots.concept: Length of the longest valid parenthesis substring
slots.objective: Use stacked indices rather than stacked symbols
slots.notRedundant: Gives the pattern a Hard tier and introduces storing positions on the stack.

slots.concept: Maximise satisfied children by matching sorted sizes to sorted demands
slots.objective: Sort both sides, then advance greedily
slots.notRedundant: interval-scheduling holds four problems but the topic never establishes the plain sort-then-scan move they specialise.

slots.concept: Minimum increments to make all values distinct
slots.objective: Prove the local choice is safe after sorting
slots.notRedundant: Introduces "why is greedy correct here" without needing a formal exchange argument.

slots.concept: Shortest clear path through a binary grid, eight-directional
slots.objective: BFS yields shortest paths on an unweighted graph; DFS does not
slots.notRedundant: All four existing graph problems are DFS/connectivity; none involves distance.

slots.concept: Minutes for a spreading state to fill a grid, or report impossible
slots.objective: Seed a BFS from many sources at once and count levels
slots.notRedundant: Multi-source BFS and level counting are distinct from single-source distance.

slots.concept: Fewest one-letter transformations between two words via a dictionary
slots.objective: Recognise an implicit graph where states are not given as edges
slots.notRedundant: The graph must be inferred rather than supplied, and the string signature keeps the pattern reachable in C.
slots.signature: string beginWord, string endWord, vector<string> wordList -> int

slots.concept: Whether a set of prerequisite pairs can all be satisfied
slots.objective: Detect a cycle in a directed graph via in-degrees
slots.notRedundant: The existing graph problems are all undirected; direction changes what connectivity means.

slots.concept: Fewest rounds needed to finish all courses when independent ones run in parallel
slots.objective: Peel the dependency graph layer by layer with Kahn's algorithm
slots.notRedundant: Turns cycle detection into a quantity, and the answer is unique so it needs no artificial ordering rule.

slots.concept: Number of monotone lattice paths across a grid
slots.objective: See a 2-D table and its base row and column
slots.notRedundant: Every existing DP problem is one-dimensional; this is the first table.
slots.int64: CONSTRAIN — the count is a binomial coefficient, so cap grid dimensions so it stays inside the exact-integer range

constraint.canonical: LeetCode allows m, n up to 100 while asserting the answer fits about 2x10^9 — those two claims are not consistent, since C(198,99) is astronomically larger
constraint.robinhood: m, n <= 20, giving a maximum of C(38,19) ~ 1.7x10^10, comfortably inside the exact-integer range
constraint.legitimate: Yes. The lesson is recognising a 2-D table with a base row and column; the magnitude of the count is incidental, and the canonical statement is self-contradictory about it anyway. Tightening the bound makes the problem MORE coherent than the original.

slots.concept: Minimum-cost path from corner to corner of a cost grid
slots.objective: Choose between predecessors instead of summing them
slots.notRedundant: Optimisation rather than counting over the same table shape.

slots.concept: Monotone lattice paths with blocked cells
slots.objective: Encode an obstacle as a zeroed state
slots.notRedundant: Teaches that a constraint becomes a base-case change, not new logic.

slots.concept: Whether an array splits into two equal-sum halves
slots.objective: Recognise subset-sum behind a partition question
slots.notRedundant: The direct DP counterpart of the recursive subset-count problem, which is how the bridge from recursion to DP is taught.

slots.concept: Smallest achievable difference between two subset sums
slots.objective: Search reachable sums rather than test one target
slots.notRedundant: Generalises a yes/no subset-sum into an optimisation over reachable states.

slots.concept: Repeatedly combine the two largest values until one or none remains
slots.objective: Use a heap for repeated extract-max
slots.notRedundant: The topic is empty; nothing in the curriculum uses a priority queue.

slots.concept: Minimum total cost to combine all lengths pairwise
slots.objective: Extract-min twice, push once, and see why greedy is optimal here
slots.notRedundant: Extract-min plus reinsertion is a different loop from extract-max, and it sets up Huffman-style merging.
slots.int64: CONSTRAIN — accumulated merge cost grows quickly; cap n and values so the total stays inside the exact-integer range

constraint.canonical: n up to 10^4 with values up to 10^4, giving a total around 10^9 — already near the int32 edge
constraint.robinhood: n <= 1000 and value <= 10^4, giving a total under about 10^8
constraint.legitimate: Yes. The lesson is extract-min twice, push the sum back, and see why the greedy choice is optimal. The accumulated total is bookkeeping. A tighter bound also keeps the answer inside int32, so every typed language uses its natural type.

slots.concept: kth largest element of an unsorted array
slots.objective: Keep a bounded heap of size k instead of sorting everything
slots.notRedundant: Introduces the size-k bound, which is the whole idea of the pattern.

slots.concept: The k most frequent values in an array
slots.objective: Compose a frequency map with a bounded heap
slots.notRedundant: Combines strings/frequency-counter with the heap bound; neither topic teaches the combination.
slots.ordering: REQUIRED — the canonical problem permits any order, which this grader cannot accept. The statement must require descending frequency then ascending value, which also makes the answer unique when frequencies tie.

learner_sequence.name: Foundations — the empty root
learner_sequence.why: basics is the declared prerequisite of all 16 other topics and holds nothing. Everything else waits on it.

learner_sequence.name: Sorting — the preprocessing step four topics assume
learner_sequence.why: arrays, binary-search, heaps and greedy all declare sorting as a prerequisite, and it is empty.

learner_sequence.name: Recursion — the shape DP is built from
learner_sequence.why: dynamic-programming declares recursion as a prerequisite and already holds four problems while recursion holds none.

learner_sequence.name: Arrays — depth on what is already started
learner_sequence.why: kadane has one problem; intervals is a first-tier pattern and empty. Intervals follows stage 2 because it is sort-then-scan.

learner_sequence.name: Binary search — boundaries, then the predicate leap
learner_sequence.why: lower-upper-bound is the discipline every other binary-search pattern reduces to; search-on-answer is the conceptual jump the topic exists for.

learner_sequence.name: Strings — before the window topic that uses them
learner_sequence.why: the corrected prerequisite direction: 14 of the window topic's problems are string-typed, and two of them need frequency counting.

learner_sequence.name: Sliding window — repair the one-problem gap
learner_sequence.why: variable-size is the most transferable window idea and had a single problem beside neighbours holding twelve.

learner_sequence.name: Bit manipulation — the groundwork under xor
learner_sequence.why: basic-bit-ops was empty while xor-properties, which builds on it, held four.

learner_sequence.name: Stack and queue — give the entry pattern a progression
learner_sequence.why: parenthesis-matching held one boolean problem; it now runs check -> quantity -> hard.

learner_sequence.name: Greedy — the base move under interval scheduling
learner_sequence.why: sort-then-greedy was empty while interval-scheduling, a specialisation of it, held four.

learner_sequence.name: Heaps — open an empty core topic
learner_sequence.why: nothing in the curriculum used a priority queue. Comes after sorting, which it declares as a prerequisite.

learner_sequence.name: Dynamic programming — the first table, then knapsack
learner_sequence.why: every existing DP problem is 1-D. Knapsack follows stage 3, since the equal-partition problem is the DP counterpart of the recursive subset count.

learner_sequence.name: Graphs — distance, then dependency order
learner_sequence.why: all four existing graph problems are DFS connectivity; nothing computes a distance or handles direction.

Already holds 61 of 96 problems. Adding more would deepen the imbalance; only the one-problem gap is repaired.
Design-shaped. CORE_INTERVIEW importance, but blocked on the signature model rather than on priority.
